column2: This coin isn't fair. It lands heads four times in five. Alice knows that. Bob only suspects it. They can still settle a bet with it, perfectly fairly, using nothing but this coin.
The obvious way is to call it. One toss, heads or tails. But in a thousand tosses, heads comes up seven hundred ninety-one times. Whoever gets heads wins about four bets in five.
Letting Bob call doesn't fix it. He doesn't know which side is the lucky one, and Alice does. Whoever knows the coin best wins.
A coin tossed and caught can't really be this unfair. A spun coin can. So can a loaded die, or the electrical noise inside a computer.
So here's the puzzle. One unfair coin. One player who knows its secret, and one who doesn't. How could they make the bet fair anyway?
Toss the coin twice, and look at the two results as a pair.
A pair can be four things. Two heads, heads then tails, tails then heads, or two tails.
Picture every way the two tosses could go as a square. The first toss splits it into a wide piece for heads and a thin piece for tails. Heads gets four fifths of the width.
The second toss splits it again, bottom to top, at the same mark, because it's the same coin.

That makes four blocks, and a block's share of the square is its pair's chance. Count the small squares. Two heads has sixteen of the twenty-five, and two tails has one. What about heads then tails, against tails then heads?
Four each. Exactly equal. Sixteen percent of the square.
Alice calls heads then tails. Bob calls tails then heads. If the pair matches, throw it away and toss two fresh ones.
A thousand games with our coin. Alice wins four hundred ninety-four. Bob wins five hundred six. A perfectly fair coin wouldn't split five hundred each, either.
The coin is as unfair as ever. The game isn't.
Why exactly equal? Heads then tails is four fifths wide and one fifth tall. Tails then heads is one fifth wide and four fifths tall.
Flip one across the diagonal and it lands on the other. The same two numbers, multiplied in the other order. And multiplying doesn't care about order.
Make the coin worse. Ninety percent heads. Are the two blocks still equal?
Yes. Nine percent each. Slide the cut anywhere, even past the middle so the coin favours tails. One block is always the mirror image of the other.
In letters, call the chance of heads p. Tails gets the rest, one minus p. Heads then tails is p times the rest. Tails then heads is the rest times p. Equal for every p.
So Bob doesn't need to know how unfair the coin is, or which side it favours. He doesn't even need to trust Alice.
The trick does lean on two things. The coin's chance is the same on both tosses of a pair. And one toss doesn't affect the next, which is what independent means.
The trick has a price. With our coin, most pairs get thrown away. A pair decides only thirty-two times in a hundred.
So how many tosses does a game take, on average?
A pair decides about one time in three, so about three pairs. That's about six tosses. Exactly, six and a quarter.
Ten thousand games agree. They average six point two one tosses.
A fair coin still averages four tosses. A coin that's ninety-nine percent heads averages about a hundred and one.

And nobody can promise when a game will stop. The longest of our ten thousand ran sixty tosses. No rule can do better. A rule that always finishes must hand an unbroken run of heads to somebody, and a coin that nearly always lands heads makes that somebody the winner.
Now break it. Toss our unfair coin first, and a fair coin second. Is heads then tails still equal to tails then heads?
No. One cut moved and the other didn't, so the blocks aren't mirror images any more. Forty percent against ten. Alice wins four games in five, as if they'd never bothered.

A sneakier break is a coin with a memory. Count this one's heads and it looks fair, but it copies its last result four times in five. After two heads, heads then tails needs one change of side, and tails then heads needs two. So it's four times as likely.
The cure is to use only the tosses that come straight after a head. Those all share one chance, so they behave like a plain unfair coin, and the trick handles that.
Back to why the trick works. Heads then tails and tails then heads hold the same results, one head and one tail, in a different order.
Try three tosses. Two tosses needed a square, so three need a cube. Here are three patterns. Two heads then a tail. Heads, tails, heads. A tail then two heads. Which is likeliest?

None. Each is four fifths, times four fifths, times one fifth, in some order. The same slab, turned three ways. For tosses like ours, with the same chance every time and no memory, order never changes a chance.
So sort every pattern by its counts, how many heads and how many tails. With two tosses the groups hold one, two and one. The middle group is our trick.
With three tosses, one, three, three, one. With four, one, four, six, four, one. You may know these numbers. It's Pascal's triangle.
The coin's unfairness decides which group you land in. But inside a group, every pattern is equally likely, however unfair the coin.
The counts carry the unfairness. The order is perfectly fair.
Look at the middle of the row for four tosses. Six patterns, all equally likely. What else has six equally likely results?
A die. Toss the coin four times. If exactly two are heads, the pattern picks the face. If not, toss four fresh ones.
Twenty-four thousand tosses of our unfair coin made nine hundred forty-nine rolls of a fair die. Each face came up about one time in six.
It isn't cheap. A coin that loves heads rarely gives exactly two in four. A roll costs about twenty-six tosses, on average.
There are cheaper rules, but the idea is what matters. Any group of patterns with the same counts is a fair choice among them.
Now swap the coin for a loaded die. This one shows a six half the time.
Alice and Bob want a fair decision from it. How would you do it?
Roll it twice. If the two rolls match, roll two fresh ones. If not, Alice wins when the first roll is bigger, and Bob wins when the second is.
It's the coin trick again. A six then a five is exactly as likely as a five then a six, and the diagonal pairs every block with its equal.
And a coin is just a die with two faces.
Three rolls do more, and three need the cube again, cut by the die's chances along every side.
Say the rolls are a four, a five and a six, in some order. Each order lands in one of these six bricks. How do the bricks compare?
They're one brick, turned six ways. A tenth, by a fifth, by a half. Same counts, same chance.
So when three rolls all differ, the order they came in is a fair choice among six. Low, middle, high. High, low, middle. Six in all. If any two match, roll three fresh ones.
Six thousand rolls of the loaded die made six hundred fifty rolls of a fair one.
It keeps going. Four different rolls can come in twenty-four orders. But rolls that all differ get rarer, so each step costs more.

The two toss trick comes from the mathematician John von Neumann, in a talk in nineteen forty-nine. The printed summary calls it rigorously unbiased, which is to say exactly fair. It also names the price. At most twenty-five percent as efficient as ordinary coin tossing.
Our coin does worse. A hundred tosses give about sixteen fair ones. Could a better rule get all hundred?

No. Guess heads and you're right four times in five, so each toss of this coin holds less than a fair one. The most any rule can average is just over seventy-two. That ceiling is called the coin's entropy.

You get closer by wasting less. Use the bigger groups in deeper rows of the triangle. Or keep what the trick ignored, which pairs matched and what the matching pairs showed, and run the trick again on those. Both climb toward the ceiling, and never quite reach it.
Computers need fair tosses too, for passwords and secret codes. They get them from electrical noise, and raw noise comes out a little lopsided. What would you do with it?
Pair the readings up, and throw away the pairs that match. In nineteen ninety-nine, one chip maker, Intel, built a corrector based on this trick into its random number generator.
So an unfair coin still has a fair one inside it, as long as it can land both ways. You find it by setting aside how many heads came up, and looking only at the order.
